results.gap_diagnosis: The current transcript reveals the teacher asking general status questions: "has anybody started the project yet?", "have you guys started cutting the foam board?", and reminding about assignment submission. This reflects passive listening and some acknowledgment from students but no evidence of individual cognitive construction or generation of new knowledge. The teacher's questions imply group-level checking rather than eliciting individual reflections or outputs. Participation appears limited to general verbal responses, with no student-generated artifacts or individual reasoning shown. The phrase "have you so you've all turned in your assignment drawing right" suggests a collective status update, indicating potential bottleneck in engaging all students individually and deeply.
results.proposed_rewrite: Modify the project check-in to require each student to independently present their current project plan or a sketch of their foam board cutting layout. This would shift the focus from general status questions to soliciting individual cognitive products, encouraging each student to mentally organize and articulate their approach before proceeding. For example, the teacher might say, 'Please finalize and submit your individual cutting plan sketch now, and briefly write a reflection on your next steps and anticipated challenges.'
results.scaffolding_strategy:
1) Individual Sketch Journals: Assign each student to create and submit a detailed sketch of their foam board cutting plan with annotations explaining their rationale, materials chosen, and sequencing. This ensures solo cognitive construction without peer influence.
2) Reflective Prompting: After submission, ask each student to write a brief personal reflection on their project progress and next steps, encouraging metacognitive engagement and individual knowledge building.
results.new_question: Can you individually describe your planned steps for cutting the foam board, including any challenges you anticipate, and provide a sketch that illustrates your plan?
results.reference_answer: I plan to first measure and mark the foam board according to the dimensions specified in the project. Then, I will carefully cut along the marked lines using the foam cutter, ensuring clean edges. My sketch shows the dimensions and the order in which I will make the cuts. I anticipate the challenge of keeping the cuts straight, so I will use a straight edge as a guide. I also plan to check the measurements twice before cutting to avoid errors.

results.gap_diagnosis: The current transcript reveals the teacher engaging students predominantly through eliciting simple verbal responses (e.g., 'okay so have any of you had trouble cutting the foam board' with some brief student signaling 'one, two, three'), which indicates passive to active engagement but no evidence of students individually producing knowledge artifacts or deeply constructing understanding. The teacher provides explanations and corrections but students are not prompted to generate their own independent outputs or reflections. This suggests bottlenecking because although many students respond nonverbally, cognitive construction is limited to the teacher's input, lacking individual student-generated work that would solidify understanding. The transcript states, 'if you have trouble you're probably using an old blade,' but no student-generated explanations or problem-solving are visible.
results.proposed_rewrite: To elevate the cognitive mode to Constructive (C), the teacher should redesign the lesson to include individual, reflective tasks where each student independently analyzes their own foam board cutting technique and documents or sketches a personalized troubleshooting plan or procedural improvement. This could involve a solo written reflection or drawing to articulate their understanding of blade condition, angle, and pressure adjustments, supported by self-assessment guided by probing questions. This reframes the learning from passive reception to active, individual knowledge construction.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1) Individual Reflection Journals: After demonstrating the cutting tips, each student independently writes a detailed reflection explaining how they will adjust their technique based on the blade condition, angle, and pressure factors, including a self-assessed plan for improvement without any peer discussion. 2) Solo Analytical Sketching: Students individually create a step-by-step diagram or annotated drawing of the optimal foam board cutting process highlighting the critical variables and personal strategies to avoid common mistakes, ensuring they produce original work and cognitive construction.
results.new_question: Can you individually describe and illustrate your personal strategy for cutting foam board effectively, including how you will adjust blade sharpness, cutting angle, and pressure, based solely on your own experience and reasoning?
results.reference_answer: Based on my experience, I will first check if my blade is sharp because a dull blade makes cutting harder. I plan to hold the blade at about a 45-degree angle to the foam board since cutting at the wrong angle can tear the board. I will apply gentle, consistent pressure and avoid pushing too hard to prevent damaging the foam. I will make two to three light passes instead of trying to cut all at once. My diagram shows the blade angle, the direction of cutting, and notes about pressure, emphasizing careful, steady strokes.

results.gap_diagnosis: The current transcript indicates the teacher is primarily providing explanations, observations, and advice to the whole class without eliciting individual student cognitive constructions. For example, the teacher says, 'so if you've turned in drawings and you're probably you know in good shape and you should probably just start cutting already,' which is directive and advisory but not eliciting student-generated outputs. Also, the teacher notes common student mistakes but does not engage any individual student in solo reflection or independent problem solving. This suggests the mode is predominantly Passive or at best Active, with no evidence of students independently constructing knowledge or creating original work during the interaction. The bottleneck is that the class size (30) and lecture-style talk limit individual student cognitive engagement, and no individualized probing or solo output tasks are present.
results.proposed_rewrite: To transition into Constructive mode, redesign the lesson so that after the teacher's explanation, each student independently creates a revised design composition sketch addressing issues like 'static symmetry' and 'continuance.' The teacher should then individually prompt students to reflect on their own work, explaining their compositional decisions in writing or drawing, without any peer interaction. This can be facilitated by providing students with a structured worksheet prompting them to identify and correct static elements and to incorporate the principle of continuance on their own.
results.scaffolding_strategy:
1. Individual Reflective Sketching Task: After the explanation, assign each student to independently create a new drawing or modify their existing design focusing on avoiding static symmetry and implementing continuance off the borders. Students must work silently and produce their own output without discussing with others.
2. Solo Metacognitive Prompting: Pose a series of written reflection questions prompting students to articulate why they positioned elements off-center and how their design creates movement. Collect these reflections individually to monitor understanding and provide personalized feedback.
results.new_question: Can you individually describe how your current design composition avoids static symmetry and how you have used continuance to make the design extend beyond the frame? Please write or sketch your explanation without discussing with others.
results.reference_answer: In my design, I avoided placing the main elements in the center to prevent static symmetry, instead shifting the focal point slightly to the left side. I added forms that extend beyond the border on the right, creating a sense of continuance. This makes the design feel dynamic, as if it continues beyond the frame, rather than being confined or 'stuck' in the middle.

results.gap_diagnosis: The current transcript reveals a primarily passive to attentive cognitive mode, as the instructor is delivering logistical information about office hours and instructing students to write down details: 'maybe you should write this down'. There is no evidence of students generating knowledge outputs independently or engaging in mental elaboration beyond note-taking. Thus, the cognitive mode is at most A (Attentive). The bottleneck lies in the unidirectional lecture format with no individual cognitive construction, as students are not prompted to internalize or reprocess the information beyond passive receipt.
results.proposed_rewrite: Transform the announcement into an individual reasoning task where each student independently creates a personalized office hours schedule plan or calendar entry based on the given information. This requires them to interpret timings and synthesize a plan that fits their constraints, fostering individual cognitive construction.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1. Immediately after announcing the new office hours, instruct each student to independently draft a weekly schedule excerpt marking the office hours they can attend, without any discussion or sharing. 2. Have students individually write a short reflection explaining how these new office hours align with their existing commitments and what strategies they will use to utilize office hours effectively, reinforcing internalization and personal planning.
results.new_question: Based on the updated office hours schedule I just described, can you individually create your own weekly plan showing which office hours sessions you will attend and explain your reasoning behind these choices?
results.reference_answer: I will attend office hours on Monday from 8 to 10 AM because I have no classes then, and on Wednesday evening from 6 to 8 PM, which fits my work schedule. I avoid Friday sessions as I have a class meeting that day. This plan allows me to maximize access to help while balancing my other commitments.

results.gap_diagnosis: Current cognitive mode is Passive (P). The instructor is mainly giving information and encouragement about office hours, e.g., 'I have to be honest you guys haven't been on fire about coming to office hours...' and describing how office hours work, but there is no evidence of individual student cognitive construction or generation of knowledge. The invitation to come and 'eavesdrop and listen or join in' encourages listening or interactive participation, but the transcript shows no active individual student cognitive output. The bottleneck is that students are not individually producing knowledge or reflections related to office hours; they remain listeners rather than independently constructing understanding. There is no indication of student-generated outputs or reflections in the transcript.
results.proposed_rewrite: To transition into Constructive mode, redesign the activity so each student independently reflects on their personal barriers and motivations related to attending office hours and creates a personalized action plan or self-generated explanation without any peer interaction. The teacher can prompt students to write or draw their own reasoning about why they have or have not attended office hours and what strategies they will personally use to engage in them moving forward. This makes the cognitive work individual and generative.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1. Individual Reflective Journaling: Ask each student to independently write a brief reflection identifying their own challenges and feelings about attending office hours, then to outline a step-by-step plan for how they will utilize office hours effectively before the next class. 2. Solo Concept Mapping: Require students individually to create a concept map or visual representation of the benefits of office hours and how they can overcome common misconceptions (e.g., 'bothering the instructor'), reinforcing personal understanding without any peer input.
results.new_question: Individually, can you describe your own reasons for attending or not attending office hours in the past, and outline a concrete personal plan for how you will make use of office hours going forward?
results.reference_answer: In the past, I haven't attended office hours because I felt like I might be bothering the instructor or that I wouldn't know what to ask. However, I realize from the explanation that the instructor welcomes questions and is available to help. My plan is to prepare two specific questions before the next office hour session, join the session solo, and take notes on the feedback I receive to improve my project work.

results.gap_diagnosis: The current transcript reflects an active teacher explanation and demonstration of the project submission process, primarily involving listening and observing by students. The teacher says, "okay so when you're ready to turn in the assignment... you click on that and... submit assignment... upload a file," which is instructional and directive. There is no evidence of students individually producing knowledge or outputs; no student responses or independent activities are mentioned. The behavior is bottlenecked because the teacher is the sole speaker guiding the steps without prompting or eliciting students to construct their own understanding or produce independent work related to submission guidelines.
results.proposed_rewrite: Modify instruction by introducing an individual student task where each student independently drafts a step-by-step personal checklist or annotated diagram that explains how to submit their project. This requires students to cognitively construct their own understanding of the submission process based on the teacher's explanation, rather than passively receiving it. The teacher could prompt students to visualize and write down the submission steps from memory or by referencing the platform interface, cultivating individual cognitive output.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1. Independent Submission Workflow Diagram: Ask each student to create a detailed flowchart or annotated sketch outlining the submission steps, emphasizing the required perspectives for project photos and file upload specifics, done entirely individually. 2. Solo Reflection Prompt: Have students write a brief reflection explaining why multiple angled photos are necessary and how they plan to organize their submission files, fostering internalization and personal ownership of the guidelines.
results.new_question: Can you individually write out, in your own words and order, each step you will take to submit your project successfully including how you will prepare your photos?
results.reference_answer: First, I will locate the project module in the course platform. Then, I will click on 'Submit Assignment' under Project One. Next, I will prepare four photos of my project taken at approximately 45-degree angles around it to show volume clearly. After that, I will upload these images as files. Finally, I will double-check that all files are attached correctly before submitting.

results.gap_diagnosis: The transcript shows the instructor mainly delivering instructions and warnings about the final project, with limited student verbal participation: 'okay so let me open it up to you guys do you guys have questions or issues or um yeah i have two questions sure'. This indicates a predominantly Passive (P) or possibly some Active (A) cognitive mode as students listen and ask clarifying questions. There is no evidence of peer-to-peer interaction, debate, or collaborative problem solving, which is required for Interactive (I) mode. The bottleneck is that student participation is narrowly limited to a couple of individual questions rather than engaging multiple students in dialogue or cooperative tasks. The behavior is mostly instructor monologue with minimal individual questioning, lacking any collaborative discourse.
results.proposed_rewrite: Transform the final project introduction into a structured interactive workshop where students must explain their project ideas aloud in small groups, critique each other's plans, and negotiate how to capture their project visually and in video. The teacher facilitates and probes individual thinking while orchestrating peer-to-peer exchanges to deepen collective understanding and shared problem solving about project documentation strategies.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1. Implement a 'project pitch and critique' session where each student presents their final project concept and media plan to a small assigned peer group; peers must ask clarifying questions and suggest improvements, ensuring active interactive dialogue. 2. Use 'think-pair-share' replaced by 'think-pair-discuss' where after individual reflection, students engage in structured partner debates about best video documentation techniques, culminating in a joint decision on how to film their project, promoting sustained peer interaction and co-construction of knowledge.
results.new_question: Can you explain your final project idea to your partner and discuss together which parts would benefit most from video versus photos? What suggestions would you give each other to improve your documentation plan?
results.reference_answer: My final project is a kinetic sculpture with moving parts. I think a video showing the motion would be essential, while photos can capture the details and structure. From our discussion, I realize I should film both the opening and closing movements clearly and maybe add a short narration to highlight key features, as my partner suggested. They also recommended ensuring good lighting to avoid blurry footage.

results.gap_diagnosis: The current transcript reveals a predominantly Passive mode where the teacher delivers instructions and material specifications without eliciting individual student cognitive construction. Evidence: "so what i would like you to get those materials as soon as you can..." and "you'll have a few days to do drawings and stuff but um i'm gonna also have you do an exercise with the wire before you start the project." Students are not shown producing independent knowledge outputs yet, indicating a bottleneck in active generation and individual sense-making.
results.proposed_rewrite: After providing material requirements, allocate dedicated time for each student to independently create a detailed materials procurement plan and individually draft preliminary wire exercise sketches or concept maps. The teacher should then individually probe students with targeted questions to elicit personal reasoning about material choices and exercise design, ensuring cognitive construction happens inside each learner's mind without peer interaction.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1) Structured Solo Reflection: After the material introduction, prompt students to independently write or sketch a detailed step-by-step plan of how they will obtain and use the materials, including potential challenges and solutions. 2) Individual Cognitive Probing: The teacher circulates and poses personalized open-ended questions to each student (e.g., 'Explain why you selected this wire type for your drawing exercise and predict how it will affect your project outcomes?') expecting students to articulate their reasoning independently.
results.new_question: Can you individually explain how you plan to acquire and prepare the materials for the wire exercise and how these choices influence your upcoming project work?
results.reference_answer: I will go to Home Depot to get the specified wire with the exact SKU number mentioned because it is flexible and suitable for making straight lines without kinks. I plan to start the exercise by practicing bending techniques on this wire to understand its properties, which will help me create precise shapes for the project. This preparation ensures I avoid materials that are difficult to work with and optimizes my project execution.

results.gap_diagnosis: The current transcript reveals predominantly passive listening and teacher explanation without evidence of individual student cognitive construction or output generation. The teacher provides detailed instructions about materials and tools but does not prompt students to independently generate ideas or reflect individually on the concepts. Transcript excerpt: 'the thing that that people ask me all the time is like oh i have some like galvanized wire can i use that and the answer is no you can't you have to use this wire because what we're trying to do is to emulate a pencil mark on a piece of paper...' shows a one-way teacher delivery. The participation breadth is limited as the teacher references a few named students placing projects ('dom has one and rachel has a one and julia has one and sir has a back nice white background') but there is no indication all students engage in cognitive output or individual knowledge construction. This creates a bottleneck: many students may be passively receiving instructions without producing independent representations or reasoning about the material.
results.proposed_rewrite: To transition this lesson into the Constructive mode, redesign the task so each student independently creates a visual or written artifact that demonstrates their understanding of why specific wire types are required. The teacher could assign an individual reflection or diagramming activity where students must justify the choice of wire and explain the functional properties in their own words or drawings. This retains the focus on materials but shifts from passive listening to active individual knowledge construction without any peer interaction.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1. Individual Concept Mapping: Each student individually sketches a concept map or annotated drawing that links the properties of different wires to their use in mimicking pencil marks, emphasizing visibility, cost, and bendability. 2. Solo Reflective Explanation: Prompt each student to write a short paragraph or record a brief audio reflection explaining why galvanized wire is inappropriate and why the specific black wire must be used, integrating the teacher’s reasoning but in their own words and structure.
results.new_question: Individually, can you explain in your own words why using galvanized wire does not work for this project, and how the black wire meets the necessary criteria?
results.reference_answer: Galvanized wire does not work because it cannot emulate the look of a pencil mark on paper, which is essential for this project. The black wire is chosen because it is visible against a white background, inexpensive, and easy to bend, making it suitable for creating the desired artistic effect.

results.gap_diagnosis: The transcript shows active teacher-student dialogue with students asking questions and receiving detailed individual feedback, e.g., on cutting round shapes and narrative titling. However, there is no evidence of student-generated outputs produced independently during class time; the interaction is dominated by teacher explanations and individual probing. Furthermore, the teacher encourages posting work and peer feedback outside class, which is interactive but not happening synchronously in class. "So I'll just first encourage you ... to post your work on the discussion board ... and then ... go ahead and start a conversation ... give your classmates some feedback" shows outside-class interaction but no in-class cognitive construction. Hence, the current cognitive mode is Active (A) because students listen and answer questions but do not individually produce knowledge constructions or artifacts during class. To reach Constructive (C), students must individually generate knowledge/outputs on their own, without any peer interaction or collaborative discussion.
results.proposed_rewrite: Design class sessions where each student independently creates a concept map or visual model of their design process and narrative during class, responding to teacher prompts individually without peer collaboration. Replace group critique with individual reflection journals or solo digital sketching exercises that require students to synthesize and represent their understanding of materials, cutting techniques, and narrative development. Scaffold these with targeted teacher probing questions that require solo cognitive output, such as 'Draw your personal design narrative and explain how your material choices support it.' This shifts the focus from listening and asking questions to individual cognitive construction.
results.scaffolding_strategy: 1. Implement an individual reflection and mapping task immediately after mini-lectures: each student sketches their own version of the design process and writes a short narrative to accompany it, submitting it to the teacher for individualized feedback. 2. Use teacher prompts targeting solo cognitive generation, e.g., 'Without discussing with anyone else, write a step-by-step plan for cutting your design shapes and how you will solve difficult cuts,' ensuring no peer interaction occurs during this task. These strategies produce independent student cognitive artifacts, fulfilling Mode C requirements.
results.new_question: Can you individually describe and sketch your design narrative and explain how you will apply the cutting techniques to realize your concept? Please do this on your own, without discussing it with anyone else.
results.reference_answer: My design narrative is about transforming simple geometric shapes into a complex organic form representing growth. I started by selecting bendable tie wire because it allows me to twist and shape easily, supporting the fluidity in my concept. For cutting, I plan to use an X-acto knife to cut approximate shapes, then sand the edges with 120 grit sandpaper to smooth curves, especially for circles. I will avoid using overly sturdy galvanized wire, as it is hard to bend. This approach reflects my narrative of flexibility and natural evolution.

results.gap_diagnosis: The transcript shows an individual student reflecting aloud on their own project sketches and plans, indicating active individual cognitive construction but no evidence of peer interaction or collaborative exchange. For example, the student says, 'i have an idea of what i want my project to be... i was kind of drawing on cold sketches that i've done...' which demonstrates internal knowledge generation and planning. However, the interaction is limited to teacher-student dialogue and self-generation, with no peer engagement or group discussion. The bottleneck lies in the participation breadth: only one student is actively verbalizing their thinking while others remain silent or passive, restricting the classroom coverage of this cognitive activity. Hence, the current mode is Constructive but bottlenecked by low participation and exclusive teacher-student dyads.
results.proposed_rewrite: Introduce a structured individual reflection and production phase where each student independently generates and documents their own project concept sketches or written reflections without peer input before any group discussion. This redesign ensures every student cognitively constructs knowledge individually to deepen understanding of academic integrity and project originality. The teacher can then follow up with individual probing questions to each student to validate their independent reasoning.
results.scaffolding_strategy:
1. Implement a silent individual reflection task where students independently write or draw their own interpretation of what constitutes cheating and how to maintain academic integrity in their projects, emphasizing original thought.
2. Use a teacher-driven one-on-one questioning routine, calling on students individually to explain their sketches or reflections orally to the teacher only, ensuring each student's cognitive construction is elicited without peer interaction.
results.new_question: Can you explain, using your own words and examples, how you plan to ensure your project work reflects your individual effort and maintains academic integrity?
results.reference_answer: In my project, I will make sure to develop all ideas and designs myself without copying others. For instance, I will create original sketches and write my own explanations rather than using someone else's work. This way, I keep my work honest and show my own understanding.
